$comment: What a router SHOULD do with a mediation response — not what either
implementation currently does. Where the two differ, the corpus asserts
the behaviour that is right on the merits and records the other as a
defect; `correct` names which side that is. A row is never expected to
agree with Go merely because Go is older.
Every case is stated as an HTTP response or a named precondition, never
as a call into either implementation, so any router that speaks HTTP can
run it. See conformance/README.md for the runner contract.

cases.why: A target that answers 200 with HTML has still accepted the message.
201 and 202 mean different things to an operator reading a trace.

divergence.basis: The status is the target's own answer. Flattening 201 and 202 to 200 discards information the router never had a reason to hold an opinion about, and an operator reading a trace cannot recover it.
divergence.go: common.Success() hard-codes StatusCode 200, so 201/202/204 all report 200 (verified at 819b390)

cases.why: The target accepted the request and declined the work: not a failure, so the breaker must not count it.

The request is wrong and will stay wrong. Breaker SUCCESS, which is counter-intuitive and right: a breaker exists to detect an unhealthy TARGET, and a target rejecting a bad request promptly is working perfectly. Counting it a failure would trip the circuit on a client bug and stop delivery to a healthy endpoint.

The one 5xx that is permanent. A target answering "not implemented" will not implement it part-way through a retry schedule, so treating it as transient is an unbounded retry that cannot succeed. Breaker success for the same reason a 404 is one: the endpoint answered, so it is healthy — it is the request it cannot serve.

history.found: This corpus. Java was letting 501 fall into the generic `status >= 500` branch and retrying a target that had said it does not implement the hook.
history.corroboration: Go reached the same answer independently in 4f2d52c, before this corpus existed. Two implementations arriving separately at the same rule is the strongest evidence available here that the rule is right.

divergence.basis: A 4xx nobody wrote a named branch for still ACK-drops the message permanently, which is the one condition the warning column encodes. Go warns on 400/401/403/404/501 and then only logs for the rest, so an operator is told about a 404 and not about a 422 — same permanence, same deletion, no notice. That is the shape of an omission, not a decision.
divergence.go: the generic 4xx fallback calls slog.Warn only, never warnConfig, so no warning is recorded (found by the Go conformance runner)

cases.why: 429 is a healthy target asking us to slow down. Neither a breaker success nor a failure.
An HTTP-date Retry-After is legal and unparsed here; falling back beats throwing.
R-57 (owner, 2026-09-02): any 5xx other than 502/503/504 means the app ran and answered — permanent rejection like a 4xx, single attempt, warning is the trace.

R-57 (owner, 2026-09-02): 'every other 5xx' is a range, not the single status 500 — an implementation that special-cases only 500 and retries every other non-gateway 5xx forever is non-conformant. 505 pins the boundary as a range.
502/503/504 say the target is not ready, not that the message is bad, so the group goes back rather than being dropped.
Neither implementation may claim the message was rejected when it cannot tell whether it was even seen.

divergence.go: DISPUTED. Reading mediator.go says a 1xx reaches the default arm as ErrorProcess(0, 30). But net/http's readLoop waits for a terminal response after any non-101 1xx rather than treating it as final, so a bare-1xx server should break the connection and yield ErrorConnection — matching Java exactly. A reproduction of Go's classifier agreed with the second reading. NOT resolved from source alone: settle it by running the Go runner against the real module.
divergence.java: ErrorConnection(0, 30) — java.net.http refuses to treat 1xx as final and fails the exchange, so classify() never sees it
divergence.basis: DISPUTED ON THE OUTCOME NAME ONLY — see `go`. Agreed on every field that decides the message's fate. Neither may claim the message was rejected when it cannot tell whether the target ever saw it. Both land on RETURN_TO_BROKER, a 30s delay and a breaker failure — identical fate for the message, which is what the row exists to pin. The differing outcome NAME is a client-library artefact, not a policy difference.

cases.why: A redirect the client did not follow is a misconfigured target, not a transient fault.

divergence.basis: Retrying reproduces the redirect every time, so the message can never be delivered as addressed — an unbounded retry that cannot succeed. Following it instead is not the fix either: 301/302/303 downgrade POST to GET and drop the body, so the target would receive nothing and the router would record a success.
divergence.go: falls through to the default arm: ErrorProcess(30) with StatusCode unset, so it retries for ever and reports status 0 (verified at 819b390)

cases.why: Nothing was learned about the message, so it must go back to the broker rather than be dropped.
Silently undeliverable: no host to call, and retrying cannot invent one.

divergence.basis: This path ACK-drops every message routed through it, permanently, and it is a configuration mistake an operator can actually fix — a target URL with no host. That is precisely the case for telling someone. Go warns on 400/401/403/404/501 for exactly this reason and then does not warn here, which reads as an omission rather than a decision: the pre-flight rejections are MORE clearly configuration errors than a 404 is, not less.
divergence.go: returns ErrorConfig silently — no warning service call, AND records a breaker SUCCESS for a rejection that never touched the network (verified at 819b390). Java skips the breaker entirely for both pre-flight paths, which is the better answer: a call that was never made is no evidence at all about the target’s health, in either direction.

divergence.basis: This path ACK-drops every message routed through it, permanently, and it is a configuration mistake an operator can actually fix — a mediation type that is not HTTP. That is precisely the case for telling someone. Go warns on 400/401/403/404/501 for exactly this reason and then does not warn here, which reads as an omission rather than a decision: the pre-flight rejections are MORE clearly configuration errors than a 404 is, not less.
divergence.go: returns ErrorConfig silently — no warning service call, AND records a breaker SUCCESS for a rejection that never touched the network (verified at 819b390). Java skips the breaker entirely for both pre-flight paths, which is the better answer: a call that was never made is no evidence at all about the target’s health, in either direction.

cases.why: No call was made, so there is nothing to say about the target that the breaker is not already saying: no metric, and the group returns rather than being dropped.
